StrategyGrowthDistributionRevenue

The trade must clear on the spot

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 20 August 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

In short: People share what they know when they get something back in the same moment. A promise of future collective value is a public-goods problem, and public goods are under-supplied: organisational researchers have described knowledge sharing as a social dilemma since at least 2002. The smartest capture designs are two-way. The system gives the person something useful at the moment of work and takes their knowledge in return, and both halves land in the same interaction. Make the return private, immediate and visible.

Key points

  • Contributing knowledge costs the contributor now and benefits the organisation later. Cabrera and Cabrera described this as a social dilemma in 2002: rational people stop paying.
  • This is a pricing problem, not a culture problem to be solved with a launch campaign.
  • Four returns clear on the spot: precedent, a gap the person had not seen, work done for them, and credit when their record is reused.
  • Reputation drives contribution more than reciprocity: Wasko and Faraj found members of a professional network contributed when it built their standing, not because they expected help back.
  • AI raises the stakes. When ChatGPT offered private answers, activity on Stack Overflow fell 25% within six months relative to comparable platforms.

The economics of a capture prompt

Every capture prompt in a decision system is a small trade. The person spends time writing down a reason, a context or an outcome. Someone else, usually later, gets the benefit. When the return to the contributor is "it will help the team", the trade does not clear.

This is not a new observation. Cabrera and Cabrera, writing in Organization Studies in 2002, framed knowledge sharing in organisations as a social dilemma of the public-goods kind. Sharing costs the contributor time and sometimes advantage, while the group benefits whether or not each person contributed. Non-contribution is individually tempting, and a few free riders can pull a group into a low-cooperation equilibrium. Their remedies were to restructure the payoffs, to show contributors their efficacy, and to strengthen group identity.

The empirical work since has refined the picture rather than overturned it. Kankanhalli, Tan and Wei's 2005 study of electronic knowledge repositories in public sector organisations found that knowledge self-efficacy and enjoyment in helping others significantly predicted contribution, while the effect of codification effort depended on context. People contribute when they believe what they know is useful and when the act itself is rewarding. Both are in the designer's hands.

So the economics are simple. The contributor pays now, the organisation collects later, and rational people stop paying. Price the trade so it clears in the session.

Four returns that clear on the spot

Precedent. The next screen shows the three most comparable prior decisions and how they turned out. This is the strongest return because it helps with the decision the person is making right now. Our explainer on decision precedent in AI covers how the precedent slot is assembled.

A gap they had not seen. "The last two decisions in this segment were reversed after the regulatory change in March." A warning delivered at the right moment is worth more than any summary. Ask for the gap, not the summary makes the wider case.

Work done for them. If the record is drafted from the memo, call or email they were going to produce anyway, and the record in turn drafts the next memo, capture costs almost nothing. The best capture is a by-product of work the person had to do regardless. This is Cabrera and Cabrera's first remedy, lowering the cost of contribution, built into the workflow.

Credit. Tell people when their record is reused. "Your note on the loan waiver was surfaced in four decisions this quarter, and two of them changed course." Few things motivate experts more than evidence that their judgment travels, and it is cheap to build. The research supports it directly. Wasko and Faraj's 2005 study of 173 members of a professional network, using recorded contributions rather than self-reports, found people contributed more when they saw it as enhancing their professional reputation. Expectations of reciprocity were not a significant driver.

ReturnWhat the person receives in the sessionWhy it clearsResearch it draws on
PrecedentThe three closest prior decisions and their outcomesHelps the decision in handPayoff restructuring (Cabrera and Cabrera)
A gapA warning about a reversal, rule change or missing factPrevents a mistake nowPerceived efficacy (Cabrera and Cabrera)
Work doneA drafted record and a drafted next memoCapture costs almost nothingLower contribution cost (Cabrera and Cabrera; Kankanhalli et al.)
CreditNotice of reuse and what it changedBuilds reputationReputation drives contribution (Wasko and Faraj)

If the honest answer to "what does the person get back?" is "it will help the team", expect the prompt to be ignored within a month.

Why AI raises the stakes

AI assistants make the trade harder to clear, not easier. A person who can get a private answer from a model has even less reason to contribute to a shared record.

The clearest evidence comes from public Q&A. Del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva and Wachs, writing in PNAS Nexus in 2024, found user activity on Stack Overflow fell 25% within six months of ChatGPT's release, relative to similar platforms where access was restricted. The decline affected users at all experience levels. The authors describe "a significant shift of knowledge from public to private domains." Inside a firm the same thing happens when staff ask an assistant instead of writing down what they decided.

The fix is the same: make contribution return something the private answer cannot. A model can draft. It cannot tell a person what their own firm decided last quarter, why, and how it turned out, unless someone recorded it. That is what the decision record is for, and why The commercial decisions worth recording starts with the decisions that recur often enough to produce precedent quickly.

Give first, then ask

The sequence matters. If you launch by asking for reasons and promise precedent later, people experience the system as a tax. Launch with the give side working, even if thin, and ask for contribution only once people are already coming back for it.

The cold-start problem is real, because precedent needs records. Solve it deliberately. Before launch, backfill ten to twenty past decisions in the target class through short structured interviews with the people who made them. It takes a few days, and it means the system has something to give on day one. Cabrera and Cabrera make the same point in their terms: a shared pool is only worth the individual cost once it reaches critical mass.

A check for every prompt

For each capture prompt in your design, write down what the person receives in the same session. If the honest answer is "it will help the team", expect the prompt to be ignored within a month. If it is "the next screen shows the three closest prior cases and their outcomes", it has a chance. If there is no same-session return, remove the prompt or move it to a moment where there is one.

Capture promptSame-session returnKeep, move or cut
Reason for a discount above bandThree closest past discounts and whether the deal renewedKeep
Closed-lost reasonPattern across the last ten losses in the segmentKeep
Free-text "lessons learned" at quarter endNoneCut, or move to the next comparable decision
Outcome of a past decisionNotice of where the record has been reusedKeep, and send the notice

Measure return visits per user per week. If they are not rising, the give side is not good enough yet. Our explainer on outcome write-back covers closing the loop so outcomes are captured as well as reasons.

What would prove this wrong. Sustained, high-quality contribution to a system that offers contributors nothing in the moment, driven by mandate alone. Some regulated settings achieve this; if they do so without quality decay, the trade is less essential than this piece claims. The research also suggests one refinement: intrinsic motives such as enjoyment in helping others do drive some contribution. They are real, but they are not something a system can rely on at scale.

lowob takeaways

  • Treat capture as a price, not a culture. The contributor pays now; make the return arrive in the same session.
  • Lead with precedent. The three closest prior decisions and their outcomes is the strongest same-moment return.
  • Build the reuse notification early. Reputation drives contribution, and the notice is cheap to build.
  • Backfill before launch. Ten to twenty interviewed decisions give the system something to offer on day one.
  • Cut prompts with no return. A prompt without a same-session return will be ignored.

Common questions

Why don't employees contribute to knowledge management systems?

Contributors pay now while the organisation collects later, so rational people stop paying. Researchers have described this as a public-goods social dilemma since 2002. It is a pricing problem, not a culture problem.

How do I get people to share knowledge in a decision system?

Give a return in the same interaction: comparable precedents, a warning they had not seen, drafting done for them, or credit when their record is reused.

Does recognition actually make people share knowledge?

The evidence says reputation matters. A 2005 MIS Quarterly study found members of a professional network contributed more when it enhanced their professional reputation, while expected reciprocity was not a significant driver.

How do I solve the cold-start problem for a decision database?

Before launch, backfill ten to twenty past decisions in the target class through short structured interviews with the people who made them, so precedent exists on day one.

Sources and notes

  • Cabrera and Cabrera, Knowledge-sharing dilemmas, Organization Studies 23(5), 2002. Theory paper; proposes interventions without testing them.
  • Kankanhalli, Tan and Wei, Contributing knowledge to electronic knowledge repositories: an empirical investigation, MIS Quarterly 29(1), 2005. Survey of public sector organisations; pre-dates generative AI.
  • Wasko and Faraj, Why should I share? Examining social capital and knowledge contribution in electronic networks of practice, MIS Quarterly 29(1), 2005. Study of 173 members of one professional network, as summarised on the linked page.
  • INET Oxford, New study reveals impact of ChatGPT on public knowledge sharing, 26 September 2024. Summary of del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva and Wachs in PNAS Nexus; public Q&A, not internal systems.
  • The returns table, prompt audit and backfill method are lowob's framework.
